title: Parents' accommodation of avoidance makes anxiety harder to treat
dek: The relief from avoidance teaches the brain ‘I can't handle this,’ making escape likelier next time. The evidence-based approach is gradual exposure to discomfort—a framework that works equally for everyday nervousness and clinical anxiety disorder.
why: Through a real letter, it distinguishes three diagnostic markers of clinical anxiety from everyday nervousness, and reveals well-intentioned parental responses that inadvertently perpetuate the anxiety cycle.
who: Parents whose children struggle with social, separation, or test anxiety; and caregivers trying to distinguish introversion from conditions requiring professional help.

points.h: Three markers distinguish everyday nervousness from diagnosable anxiety
points.body: Clinicians apply three hard metrics: functional impairment (whether anxiety disrupts daily life, like the letter-writer's daughter being picked up from school repeatedly mid-day), degree of suffering (crying, anguish), and duration (persisting weeks rather than resolving in days). All three together signal need for professional intervention—not mere introversion or temporary setback.

points.h: We use one word for two separate psychological conditions
points.body: Psychology should have distinct vocabularies for everyday nervousness and clinical anxiety disorder, but it doesn't. The word ‘anxiety’ both flattens everything and pathologizes it all. Elkins uses a water-glass metaphor: everyone is born with some baseline anxiety water; it serves a function, keeping you safe (look both ways before crossing, brush teeth before a date). Only when the glass overflows—due to genetics and other factors—does clinical anxiety disorder emerge.

points.h: The temporary relief of avoidance teaches permanent anxiety
points.body: Each time discomfort is escaped rather than faced, the brain learns: feeling better came from running away, therefore ‘I cannot handle this.’ Next time something similar arises, anxiety intensifies and avoidance becomes likelier. In the letter, the girl ducking into the bathroom and being picked up looks like relief to parents—but it reinforces ‘I'm alone, unloved, friendless.’

points.h: Exposure therapy starts with the smallest manageable discomfort
points.body: The gold-standard psychological treatment for anxiety is exposure therapy—ranking situations by distress level from least to most, starting with the easiest (greeting one classmate in the classroom), then gradually climbing, not throwing the child into full-day school as the first step. Elkins jokes her program ‘isn't a spa’—kids typically feel worse at first, which is precisely how you know the method is working.

points.h: Years of avoidance can transform ordinary anxiety into phobia
points.body: Elkins shared her own story: years in Boston and Manhattan meant she never needed to drive—not deliberate avoidance, but functionally she stopped. When she finally had to, while pregnant and terrified, it happened in Massachusetts, notorious for dangerous roads. Her solution: drive repeatedly until it felt boring—a finish line everyone can reach, but only after tolerating initial discomfort.

points.h: Parents are the real leverage point in treating child anxiety
points.body: Therapeutic rapport accounts for up to 50% of clinical outcomes, but even if a child refuses to see a therapist, parents aren't helpless. The most exciting progress of the past decade is ‘parent-directed’ treatment like Yale's SPACE program: the patient is the child, but the therapist primarily coaches parents, helping them spot well-meaning responses that accidentally reinforce the child's anxiety cycle.

points.h: Accommodation motivated by kindness perpetuates the anxiety cycle
points.body: Accommodation means parents adjusting their own behavior to reduce the child's distress—no parent sets out to fan the flames, but anxiety hijacks parents' deepest instinct to ease pain, making accommodation invisible and continuous. Research shows the more parents accommodate, the worse children's anxiety disorder tends to become; and those same parents suffer more depression, anxiety, and stress themselves—bad news for everyone.

points.h: Switching schools won't help without addressing the avoidance pattern
points.body: When parents wrestle with whether to transfer their child, Elkins is cautious, because anxiety is an ‘opportunist’—it will seize any chance to destroy one lifestyle and escape to the next. Without first addressing the underlying anxiety cycle and family accommodation patterns, a new school just teaches avoidance as the go-to coping strategy. Transfer should only come first if there's genuine, ongoing bullying, harassment, discrimination, or safety threats.

terms.def: A psychological treatment where someone gradually encounters situations that trigger discomfort, ranked least to most distressing, to reduce anxiety response over time.
When parents modify their own behavior to reduce a child's anxiety-related distress, potentially reinforcing avoidance patterns if done repeatedly.
Supportive Parenting for Anxious Childhood Emotions; an evidence-based intervention that coaches parents directly rather than treating the child, to interrupt anxiety cycles.
